title: Teresa's reform
hookLine: Teresa founds small, poor, joyful convents on dusty roads
tomorrow: John of the Cross in prison
last: TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.

cards: The convent had a parlor, and the parlor was busy. Friends dropped by. Relatives brought news.
Nuns from good families kept their comforts, and talked through the grille with visitors for hours.
One of those nuns, in the Spanish city of Ávila, was witty, warm and good company, and she enjoyed the parlor as much as anyone.
She later wrote that for a long stretch her prayer was half-hearted, pulled between God and the world. Then something in her turned, and she wanted something smaller and simpler. Her name was Teresa.

teach.b: Her idea was simple. A small house with only a handful of sisters. Poor, living on what was given.
Enclosed, so the parlor wouldn't run the day. Simple habits, and sandals instead of shoes, which is why her nuns came to be called discalced, meaning unshod. Silent prayer every day.
And joy: she wanted her sisters cheerful, not grim. Her first small house in Ávila met fierce opposition from the town and from her own order. She opened it anyway.

teach.h: ON THE ROADS IN COVERED CARTS.
teach.b: Then she took to the roads of Spain in rough covered carts, through heat and dust and mud, founding more houses. People tell a story from those journeys.
Thrown from a cart into a muddy river, she complained to God, and heard that this is how he treats his friends.

teach.h: NO WONDER YOU HAVE SO FEW.
teach.b: Her answer: no wonder you have so few. Whether or not it happened, it sounds like her. She also wrote about prayer as a journey inward through a castle of many rooms, with God at the center.
And among her papers, tradition says, was found a short poem.
In English, roughly: let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you; all things are passing, God does not change; patience gains everything; whoever has God lacks nothing; God alone is enough.
Jesus told a busy Martha, in the King James Bible: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful."
The Catholic Church names Teresa a saint and a Doctor of the Church: a reformer who made things smaller, so there would be room for the one thing.

how: Discalced Carmelite nuns still live in small enclosed communities shaped by Teresa's reform, and her short poem beginning "let nothing disturb you" is prayed and sung by Catholics and others, often as a short repeated chant.

games.q: you're Teresa, a well-liked nun in a large, comfortable convent with a busy parlor. you want more room for prayer. what do you do?
o: stay, and pray harder in the busy house.
found a small, poor house with a handful of sisters.
games.why: she founds a small, poor house in Ávila over fierce opposition, then takes to the roads to found more.

practice: Walk slowly, in your mind, through one ordinary routine, your morning or your phone before bed, noticing the steps that crowd it. Imagine it with one thing fewer, the way Teresa cut a convent down to its center.
If you pray, say her line slowly, let nothing disturb you; if you don't, let it be quiet a moment.

wordCard.voice: Teresa's reform. Small, poor, joyful houses of prayer that Teresa of Ávila founded along the roads of Spain, cutting convent life down to its center.

orig.note: Spanish (Latin alphabet, the original language of the poem): let nothing disturb you, the first line of Teresa's short poem.

carryVoice: Your line: let nothing disturb you. The week ran from Cranmer and More, through both sides' martyrs, Trent, Ignatius and Xavier, to Teresa. Another week, done.
